books.section: Unit 5: Toward the Civil War and Reconstruction (1844–1877)

stimulus.source_note: “The Mission of Commodore Perry to Japan in 1854,” Japanese scroll painting, 1854–1858, British Museum (BM 2013,3002.1 19). Public domain.
stimulus.text: A Japanese scroll painting from 1854–1858 shows an American steam locomotive on tracks, pulling a tender and a passenger car. The locomotive was a working miniature that Commodore Matthew Perry presented as a gift when he returned to Japan in 1854.

source: original; stimulus image from the shared pool, “The Mission of Commodore Perry to Japan in 1854,” Japanese scroll painting, 1854–1858, public domain
stem: The painting best supports which of the following conclusions about Perry's mission?

options.text: Japan immediately agreed to trade with the United States in 1853.
options.misconception: Perry first arrived in July 1853 and returned in 1854; the Treaty of Kanagawa was signed March 31, 1854, and it opened only two ports.

options.text: The United States forced Japan to adopt the English language.
options.misconception: Nothing in the painting or the mission concerns language; the treaty concerned ports, protection, and a consulate.

options.text: The United States displayed its technology to impress Japan.
Japan had already built its own railroads before Perry arrived.
options.misconception: Japan had no railroads in 1853; the locomotive was an American gift demonstrating new technology.

rationales.A: Perry's first visit was July 1853; the Treaty of Kanagawa came in March 1854 and opened only Shimoda and Hakodate, not general trade.
rationales.B: The mission was about ports and protection for shipwrecked sailors, not about language.
rationales.C: Perry brought a working miniature locomotive and telegraph apparatus as gifts — technology put on display for Japanese officials to see. Background: the Treaty of Kanagawa opened Shimoda and Hakodate and placed a consul at Shimoda.
rationales.D: Japan built its first railroad in the 1870s; in 1854 the locomotive was a novelty from America.
rationales.general:
1. Look at the gift. A working miniature locomotive, running on tracks, pulling a tender and a passenger car.
2. Ask what a gift like that does. It shows off what American industry can build.
3. Keep the treaty straight. Kanagawa opened two ports and a consulate; it did not open general trade or teach English.
Remember: diplomacy can run on display. Perry's train was an argument in miniature: look what our machines can do.
